meta.description: capital and largest city of Grand Est, located in the historical region of Alsace

entries.notes: Gaulish locative form appearing on first Roman milestones in the first century BC.
sources: Latinised first as Argentorate (with Gaulish locative ending, as appearing on the first Roman milestones in the first century)

entries.notes: Regular Latin nominative form used in later Latin texts.
sources: then as Argentoratum (with regular Latin nominative ending, in later Latin texts)

entries.notes: Celtic Gaulish name (nominative form) of the settlement, meaning related to silver/precious metal and fortified enclosure.
sources: the city was known as Argantorati (in the nominative)

entries.notes: First attested in Gregory of Tours c. 590, the Latin form of the Germanic new name.
sources: Gregory of Tours was the first to mention the name change... quam nunc Strateburgum vocant

entries.notes: German form of the name, in use through the medieval and modern period.
French Gallicized form of the Germanic name, the current official name.
sources: later Gallicized as Strasbourg

entries.notes: Lower Alsatian (Alsatian dialect) form of the name.
sources: Lower Alsatian: Strossburi

events.description: Roman camp of Argentoratum first mentioned; foundation of the Roman military settlement.
Battle of Argentoratum: Roman forces under Julian defeated the Alemanni.
Citizens revolted against the bishop's rule (Battle of Hausbergen); Strasbourg became a free imperial city.
Strasbourg massacre: the Jewish community was massacred during the Black Death persecutions.
Conquest of Alsace by the armies of Louis XIV; Strasbourg became a French city.
Siege of Strasbourg during the Franco-Prussian War.
Strasbourg annexed by the German Empire as part of the Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine after the Franco-Prussian War.
Strasbourg reverted to France at the end of World War I.
Strasbourg captured by German army in June 1940 during the Battle of France; formally annexed into Gau Baden-Elsaß.

sources: The Roman camp of Argentoratum was first mentioned in 12 BC

entries.notes: Western Roman Empire split formalized 285/395 but Argentoratum in the western half; using 362 (Battle of Argentoratum) as a documented anchor.
After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the region passed to Frankish rule; Strasbourg was part of Austrasia. Gregory of Tours mentions the city by 590 in the Austrasian context.
sources: tried by a synod of Austrasian bishops... then taken to the city of Argentoratum, which they now call Strateburgus

entries.notes: After the Carolingian reunification of Frankish lands under Pepin III (751), Strasbourg fell under the broader Carolingian/Frankish realm.
Treaty of Verdun 843 assigned Alsace and Strasbourg to East Francia. The Oaths of Strasbourg (842) mark this transition period.
sources: 842 (Oaths of Strasbourg)

entries.notes: Between 362 and 1262 governed by bishops of Strasbourg within the Holy Roman Empire framework; reinforced in 873 and 982.
sources: Between 362 and 1262, Strasbourg was governed by the bishops of Strasbourg; their rule was reinforced in 873 and then more in 982
In 1262, the citizens violently rebelled against the bishop's rule (Battle of Hausbergen) and Strasbourg became a free imperial city
It became a French city in 1681, after the conquest of Alsace by the armies of Louis XIV

entries.notes: French Revolution abolished the monarchy; Strasbourg remained French under the Republic.
sources: 1793 (Reign of Terror)

entries.notes: Third Republic proclaimed Sept 1870, but Strasbourg fell to Germany after the Franco-Prussian War.

sources: In 1871, after the Franco-Prussian War, the city, as part of the Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine, became German again, until 1918
until 1918 (end of World War I), when it reverted to France
Strasbourg was captured by the German army in June 1940... subsequently came under German control again through formal annexation into the Gau Baden-Elsaß
since the liberation of the city by the 2nd French Armoured Division under General Leclerc in November 1944, it has again been a French city

entries.notes: The area was inhabited since the Middle Paleolithic; by the late pre-Roman Iron Age the region was Celtic/Gaulish. The Gaulish name Argantorati attests Celtic presence at the site before Roman conquest. Closing at the Roman military foundation (-12 BC).

sources: The Roman camp of Argentoratum was first mentioned in 12 BC

entries.notes: Frankish Merovingian culture prevailed in the region after the Roman period and through to the Carolingian transition.
The Gaulish language was spoken by the Celtic population at Argentoratum before and during the early Roman period. Gradually replaced by Latin.
Latin was the language of Roman administration and military at Argentoratum from its foundation.
Latin continued as the language of the church and administration through the Frankish period, gradually giving way to Old High German and Old French dialects.
Germanic-speaking Franks and Alemans settled the region; the city's new name Strateburgus/Strasbourg is of Germanic origin.
sources: That name is of Germanic origin and means 'town (at the crossing) of roads'

entries.notes: Middle High German and then modern German were the dominant vernacular languages of Strasbourg through the medieval and early modern periods.

sources: It became a French city in 1681

entries.notes: German (Alsatian dialect) continued as the dominant vernacular language of the population even after French annexation.

sources: In 1871, after the Franco-Prussian War, the city... became German again, until 1918

entries.notes: French remained spoken by a portion of the population during German annexation 1871-1918.

sources: until 1918 (end of World War I), when it reverted to France

entries.notes: German (Alsatian) continued as a widely spoken vernacular after return to France in 1918.
Roman polytheism was the state religion of the Roman Empire during the occupation of Argentoratum.
Christianity spread into the Rhine region during the 3rd-4th centuries.
After Christianisation of the Empire, the Catholic Church became the state religion. Strasbourg was governed by its bishops from 362 to 1262, reflecting the church's central role.
sources: Between 362 and 1262, Strasbourg was governed by the bishops of Strasbourg
Strasbourg played an important part in the Protestant Reformation, with personalities such as John Calvin, Martin Bucer, Wolfgang Capito

entries.notes: After French annexation in 1681, Catholicism was re-established as dominant; Protestantism continued as a significant minority.
Protestant communities persisted after French annexation, protected under Alsatian concordat arrangements.
Jewish community re-established in Strasbourg in the post-Revolutionary period following emancipation.
The fertile area between the Ill and Rhine had already been populated since the Middle Paleolithic, per the article.

sources: The Roman camp of Argentoratum was first mentioned in 12 BC

entries.notes: Roman settlement grew around the camp during the early imperial period.
By the late Roman period Argentoratum was a significant city; Battle of Argentoratum 357 AD attests its importance.

sources: Strasbourg became a free imperial city in 1262
It became a French city in 1681
In 2016, Strasbourg was promoted from capital of Alsace to capital of Grand Est
